common_name: Bertie Ferris Daylily (Gold-Edged Orange-Red Louisiana Heirloom Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this Louisiana-bred heirloom is heat- and humidity-proven and performs especially well through Gulf South summers.

directions: Bertie Ferris was hybridized in Louisiana and is remembered as one of the earliest daylilies to show a clean, contrasting edge trait, its orange-red petals rimmed in a narrow band of gold that made it influential in the later development of modern edged and eyed daylily lines. Flowers open a rich vermillion-orange with the gold picotee brightening toward the ruffled edge, held on sturdy branched scapes above grassy clumping foliage through a long midsummer season. Because it was bred and proven in the Deep South, it shrugs off heat and humidity that stall some Northern-bred cultivars and keeps producing bloom after bloom in Gulf Coast gardens. Plant in average, well-drained soil and water during dry spells the first season; established clumps are drought-tolerant and need only dividing every three to four years when flowering slows from overcrowding.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Bitsy is one of the most reliable and long-cultivated miniature daylilies, forming dense grassy clumps that spread readily.

directions: Bitsy is a long-popular miniature daylily bearing a steady succession of small, clear canary-yellow flowers only about two inches across, produced in such abundance and over such a long season that a single clump can carry color from early summer well into fall. Its narrow, grass-like foliage stays neat and low, making it a dependable edging plant or front-of-border filler where larger daylily clumps would be too coarse. It tolerates a wider range of conditions than many daylilies, taking a few hours of afternoon shade without a major drop in bloom, and multiplies quickly into a thick, weed-suppressing patch. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the flower count high, since Bitsy is vigorous enough to become tightly root-bound faster than larger-flowered cultivars.

common_name: Blackberry Candy Daylily (Ruffled Wine-Purple Daylily with Cream-Gold Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; part of the ruffled tetraploid 'Candy' line of daylilies bred for heavily textured edges and rich, saturated color.

directions: Blackberry Candy carries deep wine-purple, almost blackberry-colored petals with a heavily ruffled cream-to-gold picotee edge and a green throat that sharpens the contrast, a tetraploid form that gives the substantial, well-textured bloom typical of the modern 'Candy' series. Scapes are well branched and hold flowers above the clumping foliage through a solid midsummer season, reblooming side shoots on established clumps. The dark, richly saturated color reads best against light-colored companions or pale groundcovers, where the ruffled edge catches the light. Grow in average, well-drained soil with full sun for the darkest color and most vigorous bloom, and divide every three to four years once clumps become crowded and flower count declines.

common_name: Always Afternoon Daylily (Stout Medal Lavender-Mauve Tetraploid Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a Stout Silver Medal winner recognized for exceptional garden performance across a wide range of climates.

directions: Always Afternoon bears large, rounded, dusty lavender-mauve flowers with a lime-green throat, a tetraploid cultivar prized for its substantial petal texture and heavy branching that keeps buds opening over a long midsummer season. It received the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for proving itself a dependable, floriferous performer in gardens well beyond its originating region. The soft, muted color combines easily with brighter daylilies and other perennials without clashing, making it a useful anchor color in a mixed border. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide overgrown clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep bloom production strong.

common_name: Prester John Daylily (Historic Tawny-Orange Daylily with Maroon Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a long-lived mid-twentieth-century cultivar still passed along in older Southern gardens for its toughness and reliable bloom.

directions: Prester John is a historic daylily dating to the mid-twentieth century, bearing tawny-orange flowers deepened by a maroon-red eyezone around a green throat, a color combination that was distinctive enough in its era to keep the cultivar in circulation among heirloom daylily collectors for decades. Clumps are vigorous and increase readily, sending up tall, well-branched scapes that hold their blooms clear of the strappy foliage through a long midsummer display. Like most older daylily cultivars it asks for very little: average, well-drained soil, full sun, and occasional division every four or so years once the clump becomes congested and bloom count drops. Its toughness and heat tolerance make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a piece of daylily history that still performs as well as many modern introductions.

common_name: Wedding Band Daylily (Cream Daylily with Gold Picotee Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a widely grown older cultivar valued for its crisp, light-catching edge pattern.

directions: Wedding Band bears near-white to pale cream flowers rimmed with a crisp, narrow band of golden yellow, a picotee edge pattern that gives the bloom a finished, ribbon-trimmed look against its pale base color. Well-branched scapes stand above clumping grassy foliage and produce flowers steadily through the midsummer season, with the edge contrast showing best in morning light before the heat of the day. It combines easily with both pastel and bright-colored companions in a mixed perennial bed, since the pale base color reads as neutral. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to maintain strong bloom production.

common_name: Spacecoast Sea Shells Daylily (Ruffled Shell-Pink Spacecoast Series Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; part of the modern 'Spacecoast' line of daylilies bred in Florida for heavily ruffled, richly textured blooms.

directions: Spacecoast Sea Shells produces soft, shell-pink to cream flowers with heavily ruffled, almost crimped petal edges and a lightly gilded throat, one of the many richly textured cultivars bred under the Florida-based Spacecoast line for gardeners in warm, humid climates. The ruffling gives the bloom a fuller, more substantial look than plain-edged daylilies, and the pale, blended coloring makes it easy to combine with brighter perennials nearby. Bred and selected in a hot, humid Gulf climate, it holds up especially well in Southern gardens where some Northern-raised cultivars can look thin by midsummer. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom count high.

common_name: Prairie Moonlight Daylily (Tall Fragrant Pale-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; one of the taller heirloom Marshall-line daylilies bred from the tall, extended-blooming Prairie series.

directions: Prairie Moonlight is a tall, older daylily cultivar bearing pale, moonlight-yellow flowers with a light fragrance most noticeable in the evening, part of a lineage of tall-scaped Marshall-bred daylilies selected for height and extended bloom time held well above the clumping foliage. Its statuesque scapes make it useful at the back of a mixed perennial border or massed along a fence line, where the soft yellow glows in low evening light. Established clumps are vigorous and tolerate heat and average garden soil without complaint, needing only routine watering during dry spells. Divide congested clumps every four or so years in spring to renew vigor and bloom count once flowering begins to taper off.
